html:
Markov random field on a lattice
Full Markov random field
Both layers together. Click any white node to see its Markov blanket.
Model layer
Nodes are drawn white as in the printed figure. Tick the box (or move β) to shade each state by its smoothed value.
β = 0 : each state follows its own observation.
β large : neighbours agree, the field becomes smooth.
Click a white node in the figure to reveal its Markov blanket.
⚠ Figure failed to load

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line drawing of a graphical model laid out as a two-dimensional lattice in oblique projection, built from two kinds of nodes. Open white circles occupy the lattice sites, arranged in three receding rows of three visible sites each; within a row they are joined by horizontal edges that run past the rightmost circle to the frame edge, and between rows by short diagonal edges slanting down and to the left, which likewise continue off the lower-left corner, so the grid reads as a fragment of an unbounded array. A single vertical edge rises from each white circle to a solid gray filled circle, one gray node per site, drawn above and slightly behind its partner. Only the back row carries labels: its white circles are marked with the boldface symbols x_1, x_2, and x_3, and the gray circles directly above them y_1, y_2, and y_3. Because every gray node hangs off exactly one white node while the white nodes alone form the grid, the drawing separates per-site attachments from neighbor-to-neighbor coupling. The structure depicts a Markov random field over a spatial grid, each site carrying a state variable tied to its four lattice neighbors.

elements: 3×3 lattice of open white circles (hidden state sites x), arranged in three rows receding up-and-right along the oblique depth direction
Horizontal black edges joining the three white circles within each row (row-internal neighbor coupling)
Horizontal edge stubs continuing past the rightmost white circle of each row to the frame edge (lattice continues unbounded)
Diagonal black edges joining each white circle to the corresponding white circle in the row in front of it (slanting down-and-left)
Diagonal edge stubs continuing off the lower-left from the front-row circles (lattice continues unbounded)
Nine solid gray filled circles (observations y), one per lattice site, drawn above and slightly behind its white partner
Nine short vertical black edges linking each white circle to its own gray circle
Boldface labels x_1, x_2, x_3 to the upper-right of the three back-row white circles
Boldface labels y_1, y_2, y_3 to the upper-right of the three back-row gray circles

interactions.teaches: The Markov blanket of a site: conditioned on its four lattice neighbors and its own observation, a state is independent of the rest of the field.
Stronger pairwise potentials pull neighboring hidden states toward the same value, producing spatially smooth labelings while the fixed observations resist.
interactions.label: Coupling strength β between neighboring x

demo_steps.title: The hidden lattice
demo_steps.narration: Only the white state nodes and their grid edges are shown: every site is coupled to its four nearest neighbors, and the edges run off the frame because the field is unbounded.

demo_steps.title: Per-site evidence
demo_steps.narration: Now only the vertical links appear: each gray observation y hangs off exactly one white state x, so evidence enters the model one site at a time.

demo_steps.title: Full Markov random field
demo_steps.narration: Both layers together. Click any white node to see its Markov blanket — four neighbors plus its own observation — while every other edge fades.

demo_steps.title: Weak coupling
demo_steps.narration: With β near zero each state follows its own observation independently; the shading of the white nodes is noisy and uncorrelated across the grid.

demo_steps.title: Strong coupling
demo_steps.narration: Raising β makes neighboring white nodes converge to similar shading — the field becomes smooth — even though the gray observations never change.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Oblique projection: +X is screen-right (true horizontal), +Y screen-up (true vertical), +Z the receding diagonal drawn up-and-to-the-right at roughly 40° from horizontal with ~0.55 foreshortening. Lattice sites at X = 0, 2.6, 5.2 (columns 1-3) and Z = 0, 2.6, 5.2 (front row to back row), all at Y = 0. White circles: radius 0.5 world units, fill #FFFFFF, stroke #000000, stroke weight ~0.09 units (heavy, as in source). Gray circles sit at the same X and Z + 0.35, at Y = +2.4 above their white partner; radius 0.5, fill #808080, stroke #000000. Vertical connector from white node top to gray node bottom, black, same weight as node strokes. Row-internal horizontal edges span X between adjacent columns; each row's edge also extends +2.6 units past the rightmost (column-3) node toward the frame edge and is cut there. Diagonal inter-row edges connect (col, row r) to (col, row r-1) i.e. slant down-and-left on screen; the front row additionally carries stub edges continuing 1.8 units further down-left off the lower-left corner. Labels only on the back row (Z = 5.2): bold serif 'x_1', 'x_2', 'x_3' placed immediately up-and-right of each back-row white circle; bold serif 'y_1', 'y_2', 'y_3' immediately up-and-right of each back-row gray circle. Text black, height ~0.7 units. Whole figure spans roughly X ∈ [-2, 11], Y ∈ [-2, 4]. Coupling slider maps to node fill lightness: each white node's fill interpolates from its own random observation value (β=0, grays vary independently, fill lightness 60-100%) toward the lattice mean (β=3, all nodes nearly identical lightness) via one sweep of mean-field/ICM update s_i ← (y_i + β·Σ_neighbors s_j)/(1 + β·n_i); gray node fills never change.
interactionPlan.notes: Render in Three.js with an OrthographicCamera plus a custom oblique shear matrix (cabinet projection: x' = x + 0.55·z·cos40°, y' = y + 0.55·z·sin40°) rather than an orbiting camera, so the figure keeps the source's flat oblique read; no orbit interaction is offered. Draw nodes as flat circles (CircleGeometry facing camera) with a separate ring mesh or LineLoop for the heavy black outline so stroke weight stays constant. Edges as Line2/LineMaterial fat lines (uniform ~3px screen width) since thin THREE.Line ignores linewidth. Draw order: edges first, then nodes on top (renderOrder / depthTest false) so circles occlude the lines, matching the line-drawing look. Labels as CSS2DRenderer HTML spans with MathJax-style italic subscripts. Click picking via raycaster on the white circle meshes only; on selection, set non-blanket edges and nodes to opacity 0.15 and stroke the blanket edges in a highlight color (#1f77b4) while keeping the selected node's ring thicker. Toggle animates opacity of the two edge groups (grid edges vs vertical y-links) and the gray node group. Slider recomputes node fill colors each frame from a fixed random seed for the observation values so the pattern is stable while β changes. Flat white background, no lighting needed — use MeshBasicMaterial throughout.

authoredContext:
To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a Markov random field (MRF):

Two-dimensional Markov random field.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in the figure, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (the figure [a]). The figure [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red. (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.

discrepancies: Only one label ("x₁") is actually rendered; the source's x₂, x₃ and y₁, y₂, y₃ labels are absent from the view, so the key naming of the state/observation layers is lost.
The single visible label is much smaller and lighter than the source's large bold serif annotations, which are a prominent part of the original figure.

Gray observation nodes are offset in depth (GZ = -0.35), so several of them crowd or nearly collide with the white node behind them (e.g. the gray disc sitting right against the x₁ node); in the source every gray node sits cleanly above its own white node on a strictly vertical stem.
The lattice is rendered small and off-centre in the viewport, leaving large empty areas, whereas the source fills the frame with the lattice.
Node-fill grey-level shading driven by the β slider (mean-field smoothing) introduces visual states not present in the source, where all state nodes are uniformly white.
evaluation.notes: The lattice topology, oblique projection, edge stubs, and two-layer white/grey node composition closely match the source and the interaction set (layer toggles, guided steps, coupling slider, click-to-show Markov blanket) is rich and conceptually sound, but five of the six source annotations (x₂, x₃, y₁–y₃) fail to appear and the one that does is too small, badly weakening the figure's readability.
action_items: Fix the label registration — the custom {entry, group, test} objects pushed into the scaffold's `labels` array appear to break rendering for all but one label; keep a separate array for fading state and verify all six labels (x₁–x₃, y₁–y₃) appear on the back-row nodes.
Increase label font size (≈26–30px, bold serif) to match the source's prominent annotation hierarchy and place them just to the upper-right of each back-row node without overlapping the discs.
Set GZ ≈ 0 (or reduce it) so grey observation nodes sit directly above their white partners on vertical stems and no longer collide with nodes of the row behind.
Increase heightFraction / re-frame the camera so the lattice fills more of the canvas instead of occupying only the lower-left quadrant.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line drawing of a graphical model laid out as a two-dimensional lattice in oblique projection, built from two kinds of nodes. Open white circles occupy the lattice sites, arranged in three receding rows of three visible sites each; within a row they are joined by horizontal edges that run past the rightmost circle to the frame edge, and between rows by short diagonal edges slanting down and to the left, which likewise continue off the lower-left corner, so the grid reads as a fragment of an unbounded array. A single vertical edge rises from each white circle to a solid gray filled circle, one gray node per site, drawn above and slightly behind its partner. Only the back row carries labels: its white circles are marked with the boldface symbols x_1, x_2, and x_3, and the gray circles directly above them y_1, y_2, and y_3. Because every gray node hangs off exactly one white node while the white nodes alone form the grid, the drawing separates per-site attachments from neighbor-to-neighbor coupling. The structure depicts a Markov random field over a spatial grid, each site carrying a state variable tied to its four lattice neighbors.

elements: 3×3 lattice of open white circles (hidden state sites x), arranged in three rows receding up-and-right along the oblique depth direction
Horizontal black edges joining the three white circles within each row (row-internal neighbor coupling)

Diagonal black edges joining each white circle to the corresponding white circle in the row in front of it (slanting down-and-left)
Diagonal edge stubs continuing off the lower-left from the front-row circles (lattice continues unbounded)
Nine solid gray filled circles (observations y), one per lattice site, drawn above and slightly behind its white partner
Nine short vertical black edges linking each white circle to its own gray circle
Boldface labels x_1, x_2, x_3 to the upper-right of the three back-row white circles

interactions.teaches: The Markov blanket of a site: conditioned on its four lattice neighbors and its own observation, a state is independent of the rest of the field.
Stronger pairwise potentials pull neighboring hidden states toward the same value, producing spatially smooth labelings while the fixed observations resist.

demo_steps.narration: Only the white state nodes and their grid edges are shown: every site is coupled to its four nearest neighbors, and the edges run off the frame because the field is unbounded.

demo_steps.title: Per-site evidence
demo_steps.narration: Now only the vertical links appear: each gray observation y hangs off exactly one white state x, so evidence enters the model one site at a time.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Oblique projection: +X is screen-right (true horizontal), +Y screen-up (true vertical), +Z the receding diagonal drawn up-and-to-the-right at roughly 40° from horizontal with ~0.55 foreshortening. Lattice sites at X = 0, 2.6, 5.2 (columns 1-3) and Z = 0, 2.6, 5.2 (front row to back row), all at Y = 0. White circles: radius 0.5 world units, fill #FFFFFF, stroke #000000, stroke weight ~0.09 units (heavy, as in source). Gray circles sit at the same X and Z + 0.35, at Y = +2.4 above their white partner; radius 0.5, fill #808080, stroke #000000. Vertical connector from white node top to gray node bottom, black, same weight as node strokes. Row-internal horizontal edges span X between adjacent columns; each row's edge also extends +2.6 units past the rightmost (column-3) node toward the frame edge and is cut there. Diagonal inter-row edges connect (col, row r) to (col, row r-1) i.e. slant down-and-left on screen; the front row additionally carries stub edges continuing 1.8 units further down-left off the lower-left corner. Labels only on the back row (Z = 5.2): bold serif 'x_1', 'x_2', 'x_3' placed immediately up-and-right of each back-row white circle; bold serif 'y_1', 'y_2', 'y_3' immediately up-and-right of each back-row gray circle. Text black, height ~0.7 units. Whole figure spans roughly X ∈ [-2, 11], Y ∈ [-2, 4]. Coupling slider maps to node fill lightness: each white node's fill interpolates from its own random observation value (β=0, grays vary independently, fill lightness 60-100%) toward the lattice mean (β=3, all nodes nearly identical lightness) via one sweep of mean-field/ICM update s_i ← (y_i + β·Σ_neighbors s_j)/(1 + β·n_i); gray node fills never change.
interactionPlan.notes: Render in Three.js with an OrthographicCamera plus a custom oblique shear matrix (cabinet projection: x' = x + 0.55·z·cos40°, y' = y + 0.55·z·sin40°) rather than an orbiting camera, so the figure keeps the source's flat oblique read; no orbit interaction is offered. Draw nodes as flat circles (CircleGeometry facing camera) with a separate ring mesh or LineLoop for the heavy black outline so stroke weight stays constant. Edges as Line2/LineMaterial fat lines (uniform ~3px screen width) since thin THREE.Line ignores linewidth. Draw order: edges first, then nodes on top (renderOrder / depthTest false) so circles occlude the lines, matching the line-drawing look. Labels as CSS2DRenderer HTML spans with MathJax-style italic subscripts. Click picking via raycaster on the white circle meshes only; on selection, set non-blanket edges and nodes to opacity 0.15 and stroke the blanket edges in a highlight color (#1f77b4) while keeping the selected node's ring thicker. Toggle animates opacity of the two edge groups (grid edges vs vertical y-links) and the gray node group. Slider recomputes node fill colors each frame from a fixed random seed for the observation values so the pattern is stable while β changes. Flat white background, no lighting needed — use MeshBasicMaterial throughout.

discrepancies: The gray observation discs of the middle/front rows land directly on top of the back-row white state nodes (visible collisions at x₁ and x₂), whereas in the source every gray node sits cleanly in open space up-left of the next row — the stem length vs. row depth offset is mis-tuned.
Because of that collision the 'x₁' and 'x₂' labels are partly covered by gray discs, while in the source both are clearly legible to the upper-right of their white nodes.
Vertical y-stems are noticeably shorter relative to lattice spacing than in the source, compressing the two layers and reducing the clear separation between the observation row and the state lattice.
The front-row depth stubs and left horizontal stub are shorter/less prominent than in the source, where the lattice visibly runs off the bottom-left and left edges of the frame.
evaluation.notes: Composition, oblique lattice view, white/gray node scheme and off-frame edge stubs closely reproduce the source with a rich, conceptually apt interaction set (layer toggles, step tour, coupling slider, Markov-blanket picking), but the gray observation discs collide with the back-row white nodes and obscure the x₁/x₂ labels because the y-stem length is too short relative to row depth offset.
